utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone and to you, Mr. Jovic, especially. May I remind you that you took an affirmation to tell the truth, which still is binding. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours; good morning Mr. Jovic. WITNESS NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Re: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Friday evening when we concluded, you were telling the Trial Chamber how the shop you were working in had to close for several days in about November, October, November 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the shop reopen and how were you able to reopen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the shop reopened after the intense attacks had been over, which had gone on for five or six days. Following those attacks, a convoy arrived, a Libertas Convoy, led by the then president of Yugoslavia, Stjepan Mesic. This convoy arrived in Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there. What I'm actually asking you about, Mr. Jovic, is physically how and why did you reopen the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reopened for the citizens, for people living in the Old Town, because it was the only shop in the Old Town. We had to reopen, and we had an obligation to the Dubrovnik authorities to reopen because we were the only shop selling bread in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had changed that allowed you -- that enabled you to reopen the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the heavy attacks that had gone on for five or six days where there had been a lot of destruction and people had been killed, those attacks had stopped and probably a cease-fire of some sort had been signed, although there were still ongoing attacks on the outskirts of town, but we kept on working. We'd go to work early in the morning. There was no light, no electricity. We were using a generator in the Old Town for the fridge. We'd bring bread in as well as all the other supplies that we'd kept at the shop and in other parts of the town. We'd bring it there and we'd sell it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What I want to move to now is the 6th of December. You told the Trial Chamber on Friday that you were living in Gruz. Were you living in Gruz and staying in Gruz on the night of the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I always lived in Gruz, and I still do. On that particular morning, the 6th of December, we rose early, about 5.00 in the morning, because my sister and I worked. We went to work together, and we drove down to Gruz where we had another shop, and next to it there was the caddy driver. He slept there. He drove the supply van, and we went to work together because the town's transport had ceased to operate. We rose early in the morning, and we heard sounds of shooting, which was slightly unusual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went from Gruz to the other shop. Where was the other shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said the shop in Gruz next to which our driver slept -- or lived, rather, and then we went to the Old Town, to our shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you heard the sounds of shooting. Did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. The morning of the 6th of December was slightly unusual. The shooting began early. That was unusual. It was still dark, there was no light in the town. You could see them flying over us, because just behind our flat there is Mount Srdj. These were probably illumination bullets or whatever they're called. They flew from one side to the other and that was slightly unusual. Those were no direct threat to us at the time because no projectiles were landing around us. We went to Gruz, we got bread from the bakery, and got into the van, the caddy, and we drove to the Old Town. At half past five, quarter to six, intense shooting had begun all over town. You could hear sounds of both light and heavy arms firing. This grew in intensity around 7.00 in the morning. The first shells began falling on the Old Town of Dubrovnik. By that time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when the first shells started falling on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing at the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the usual things. We'd usually open around 6.00 in the morning, and customers who lived in the Old Town started coming because many people were staying inside the Old Town at the time. They would come to get bread, especially the elderly people. They used to come a bit earlier. They were afraid to come later. They'd just come early, get their bread, and go back to the shelter. That morning, the same as usual, people would come, and then shells started falling on the Old Town. And several people were in the shop by the time the shells started falling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who else was in the shop with you when the shells started falling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, my sister was there, the late Tonci Skocko and Mato Skocko, and four or five other people, our customers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you described Mato Skocko as the owner of the shop. How old was he then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mato Skocko was the manager. He ran the shop. He must have been around 45 at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your sister, how old was your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sister was 23 at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your sister a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mato Skocko a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Tonci Skocko, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think 18 or 19. Nineteen years of age at the time, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These elderly men and women -- sorry, elderly people who were coming to the shop to buy bread, what age are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those people, as a rule, were the ones who came the earliest. They were, as a rule, between 50 and 70 years of age. And then later on younger people would come that were in the Old Town, children sometimes too, but those who came first, earliest in the morning, were usually elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the elderly people a mixture of men and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they appear to you to be civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only did they appear to me to be civilians, they were civilians, those elderly people. The younger people too, probably, because had they been soldiers, they would probably have been elsewhere in positions on that day. They were most probably civilians, therefore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the children? What ages were the children who came to the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The children, between 7 and 15, I'd say. Their parents would send them, too, to go out and get bread, those who had not left town by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were children still coming to the shop in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe the shelling when it -- the intensity of the shelling around 7.00 a.m. when you said there were elderly people coming to the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first shells that resounded nearby, we weren't even aware that those had fallen on the Old Town because we were inside the shop working, but the sounds of firing got closer and closer. So people who kept coming in were stunned and told us that shells had begun to fall all over the Stradun, the fountain, and St. Blaise Church. And then the shooting kept inching closer and closer to us, and it kept growing in intensity. So at one point, when the attack was the heaviest, there would be five or six shells landing at the same time all over the Old Town, so that the whole town had been under attack, the Old Town. The phone lines had been cut. The rest of my family were back in Gruz, and we didn't know what was going on over there, whether they were still alive and how heavy the attacks were over there. It was a very difficult time for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to describe for the Trial Chamber the atmosphere in that shop when the shells were falling on the Old Town that morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, there were a few of us there, and buyers, too, who remained in the shop. One of them was a well-known painter, Josko Skerlj, who happened to be in our shop at the time, and some other people. We were all stunned and appalled listening to the sounds that were reaching us, waiting to see what would happen, because our fate was far from certain at that time. We couldn't know for sure that our shop would not be hit, whether we would survive or not. The shelter was a little further off, but we couldn't leave our shop to go to the shelter. It wasn't possible. So at about 8.00, when the first shell landed nearby --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come to that in a moment. When you're saying -- I withdraw that. You just referred to Josko Skerlj, a well-known painter. Was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said "we" a moment ago, were you referring to yourself, Tonci Skocko, Mato Skocko, and the other customers who were in the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in the shop were you -- did you go to during the first phase of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the whole thing began, the customers who remained inside the shop - and then people stopped coming into the shop at one point because it wasn't possible for anyone to reach us - we shut the door. The shop has about 100 or 120 square metres. It only has a door and a window facing the street. The other side of the shop, there is a house on the other side, and there was a small section of the shop there is a terrace and there's a garden outside, and there was some sort of a wine cellar over there where we took shelter at the time. We felt that that would be the safest place for us to be at the time, in that section of the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened -- sorry, where did you go or what were you going to tell us about at about 8.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At about 8.00, that was when the first shell landed, but shells were raining all around us. And this one landed just outside our door on the street. The explosion was powerful. There was a bang and the door opened wide. Shrapnel were flying around the shop. The till was shattered and so was the door. There was a lot of dust in the air and for a while we didn't know where we were. When the whole thing gradually settled down, when the dust settled, sounds of firing still kept resounding all around us and we regained our composure. One of our clients went outside, just outside the door onto the street, and he said that the house just next to the school building where the shelter was was on fire. The late Tonci Skocko and myself then went --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just -- I'll come to that in a moment. I just want to go back to the shelling. You said a shell landed outside and you said there was a powerful explosion. Did you see any smoke or any fire in the explosion? Can you describe to the Trial Chamber what the explosion entailed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult to describe to someone who did not experience it directly. At one point I only saw -- well, we didn't see the fire. We only saw the fire once the door was opened. There was a lot of dust. Stones were flying around as well as shrapnel. It's just slightly difficult to describe what it looked like at the moment. You don't know where you are at that moment. You have no idea what's going on. It's a very small room, and it became very musty due to the dust and everything in the air and we were happy to still be alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe the sound, the intensity of the sound of that explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's very difficult to describe the sound and whole thing happening. I don't think anyone who did not directly experience it can possibly describe it. It's a dreadful thing. You hear the powerful explosion, a bang, and when the whole thing happened, there was a lot of dust inside and smoke, and you have no idea what's happening. So first we looked at each other just to check that everyone was okay, and once we made sure, we sort of began to regain our composure, and we waited for the dust to settle. There was no light inside the shop because there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come to you going outside in a moment. I just want to concentrate at the moment on that explosion outside the shop. You said you saw fire once the door was opened. I want you to describe to the Trial Chamber the fire you saw, the size of the fire or the intensity of the fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a conflagration. I'm not sure how to say it. When a shell falls -- I was there, and I looked on. It's a flash. It's difficult to describe what it feels like when something like that is happening nearby. You just can't believe it. You don't know what to do. It's a huge flash, and then there's a powerful explosion, and then there's a lot of dust in the air suddenly and smoke. So the whole thing was quite horrifying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and the other people in the shop experience fear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't only fear. We didn't know at the time whether we were still alive. We believed ourselves to be sheltered at the time, but this was no reliable shelter. Not everyone could fit inside the shop, and we didn't know at the time whether we were all still there and still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did you and Tonci do when there was a lull in the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't really a lull, but, rather, the smoke and the dust settled inside the shop, but there was still shooting going on, firing, all over the town, powerful explosions all the time. Someone went outside and tried to cross the street to the house just opposite, to the house near the elementary school building. The late Tonci and I then went outside, although Mato had told us to stay put and not go out, but we were just curious, so we had to go out and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned there being a shelter across the street. How far in metres was this shelter from the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the shop, perhaps about 40 or 50 metres, just down the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the elementary school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a shelter in the elementary school building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This structure, this building, all the houses in the Old Town had been made the same way. It's all wooden floors and the roof, no concrete. So none of those houses were safe. But this elementary school building had been rebuilt just before the war and two floors were added, so there were a couple of concrete slabs. On the ground floor, probably, the civilian authorities had said that there should be a civilian shelter. Those civilians were elderly people who lived in the Old Town. Some of them even spent their nights there. They wouldn't even go home. They stayed there for months. Some people just came to spend the day there. So in the morning, probably the shelter was filled to capacity with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people. This was the only civilian shelter, this and the Revelin fort inside the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you and the other people in the shop go to this shelter some 40 to 50 metres away when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We couldn't. We weren't sure it would be safe to run across the street because of the shells. And our customers were there as well, and we thought that it would end soon, that it would be over shortly. But then when the attacks started in earnest, we were really afraid to go out in the street and run, because one couldn't be sure that the shell wouldn't land, so that we just remained in the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to when you and Tonci went outside. How far did you go and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went out through the door, and there was a staircase leading out into the street from that door. So we went that way. Perhaps we -- some of us lit a cigarette, and there across from the street where the shelter was, a roof on the house was on fire, the house was already on fire, and it was ablaze. At that moment, we saw a civilian who had ran across the street -- who had run across the street and into the shelter as we were looking on. And all this lasted a minute, a minute or two, perhaps, during the time that we stayed in the street. At a certain point, something happened that we -- that even -- at this point of time I am unable to find the words to describe how this had happened. That is to say at a certain point there was a huge flash followed by an explosion. There was dust, there was smoke, there was stones, there was rubble. At that time, as we were standing in the doorway next to the staircase, I and the late Tonci ran into the shop. He -- he first and then I followed him. And from the door to perhaps this distance, we -- we covered the ten metres, the length of the shop, to cross over to the other side, to this small wine cellar, as I already mentioned, which was there which we used as a shelter. And there was a counter there where we had samples of our wine while we still had wine. By that time, there was none. The late Tonci was in front, and I followed him. When we came to this counter -- behind the counter, rather, Mato Skocko said to me, "Nikola, you are wounded." I wasn't even aware. I didn't feel that I had been wounded with all the fear --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. I'll ask you about your wounding in a little while, but I just want you to concentrate on Tonci at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at that moment when Mato Skocko said this to me, I fell. I saw blood at that moment -- rather, Tonci Skocko fell on the floor at that moment, and all of us looked on, unaware what had happened. We thought that this was because of the shock that he had suffered, the impact of the shell. We were not really clear about what was really going on. So we called out to him, tried to resuscitate him. We gave him a few slaps in the face but all in vain. One of the customers who happened to be there who was somewhat knowledgeable in these matters tried to give him artificial respiration, but all this to no avail, because -- and of course at that moment none of us actually knew that he was dead. So this went on for about half an hour, and we also poured some water on him and squeezed some lemon juice in order to help him, but he was already dead, and we were not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long -- how long did this go on for? How long -- how long did you attempt to revive Tonci for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for certainly half an hour, perhaps more. This is the time that we spent trying to resuscitate him, because we thought that he was in shock and that these were the consequences of that shock that he had experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about this shelling? Was this shelling still going on in this half an hour or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes, it was. The shelling was still going on. And perhaps, in fact, the heaviest attacks were taking place at that time, about 8.00 or 9.00, when the whole city was ablaze and in smoke, and shells were landing. It was really horrific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mato do after about half an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he saw that all our efforts were to no avail, he said that he was going to get his car which was outside the Old Town in the Ploce area. We all tried to dissuade him, to tell him that he shouldn't go because of the situation, because his father, but he wouldn't listen to us. He went out, and we then turned again to Tonci, tried to resuscitate him, give him artificial respiration and calling out his name. There were a few women there who were crying out loudly because they were not aware of what was really happening. At the moment when Mato returned, he drove his car through the Skalina, the streets, actually the stairs, the steps, and his tires were totally deflated so that he actually drove on the tire rims. We were all there when Mato came flying into the shop. We took Tonci's body and took it out and into the car. As we were taking his body into the car, I went out, I went to the back side to open the back door to put him on the back seat. The late Tonci was in this jersey, in this T-shirt, and as we were trying to put him on the back seat, the T-shirt was caught in the door, and I saw a small hole in the T-shirt, perhaps the size of a -- on the chest. It was on the -- the size of a grain of corn. I didn't say anything to Mato at that point. And then Mato drove the car away through the Stradun which I think can be seen -- or his car can be seen on the photographs which were taken on that date there where the shelling took place. So he took him to hospital. Then I told the rest of the people what I had noticed. This was the way it was. And later, when Mato returned some two hours later, when he returned from hospital, he said that Tonci was dead and that he had died instantly when the -- when the shelling took place because a shrapnel had hit -- a fragment had hit him directly in the heart at that moment and perhaps his life could have been saved only in hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When his T-shirt was rolled up and you saw a small hole in his chest, did you see any blood there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no blood, interestingly enough, no blood at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to describe for the Trial Chamber Mato's reaction and his demeanour when he was there with his son who was unconscious when he went to get his car. How would you describe his reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you can imagine a person to -- who saw this happening to his own son. You can imagine what kind of a reaction he had. From the very beginning, since this whole thing started happening, not only I myself but everybody else, including Mato, thought that this was the effect of shock, of the shock, and that Tonci would recover. However, as time passed by, he probably became increasingly aware of what was really happening and that there was something wrong, so that panic set in. First of all, these ladies started crying even before they knew that Tonci was dead. And the demeanour of his father is something which is also hard to describe. It is the demeanour of a father whose son is dying in his arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll take you back now to your own injury. You said when you were there and Tonci -- people were trying to revive Tonci, someone told you that you had blood on you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I noticed that there was blood on me, nothing actually -- I felt no pain at all, but then I wasn't paying attention to -- much attention to my own wound at that time because it was still fresh, as it were. Only later, after we had taken Tonci away, and as every shop had a first aid kit including bandages and alcohol, so we dressed my wound in the -- which was in the chin and leg area, and bandaged it. These were just surface wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Did you have those wounds before you went out and there was a huge flash and the explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the chin and the right shin, right shank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of injury did you receive on your chin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a cut. It was a cut caused by the grazing of a shrapnel fragment, and it was obvious on three spots in the chin area. And also in my leg where it cut -- cut through the trouser leg and my own skin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any scars as a result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just stand up and show the Trial Chamber firstly the scars under your chin -- firstly, how many scars are there under your chin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many on your leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, can you just stand up and show the Trial Chamber, if you can, firstly the scars on your chin and, secondly, the scar on your leg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Might he approach the Bench, Your Honours? It may not be possible to see them from that distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can see where he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stand where you are. Just put your chin up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now the leg. He's demonstrating a mark midway between knee and ankle on shin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Your Honours see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you -- I think you said you bandaged it in the shop; is that correct? Your injuries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the shop after bandaging your injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after we left the shop, it was about 11.30, about midday, after all the attacks had stopped, after the shelling had abated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how long after Tonci -- Mato had taken Tonci to the hospital did you leave the shop? I appreciate it's a long time ago; approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when Mato left the hospital -- I mean the shop, he returned in about 45 minutes. He returned because the hospital was in the area between the Old City and Buninovo. It was perhaps 2 kilometres away from the Old City. So Mato, after taking his son to the hospital and after he had been examined by doctors who established death, he left the hospital and returned to the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is about how long after he took Tonci to the hospital and came back, did you leave the shop? What sort of period was there between him leaving for the hospital and you leaving the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps around three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go when you left the shop, and did you leave with your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We left the shop. Mato Skocko went with this other person, Josko Skerlj, I believe, and perhaps some other people as well. They went to Mato's house because he was unable to go alone, and his wife, the mother of the late Tonci, didn't know at the time at all that Tonci had been killed. I and my sister went to our own house through the Pile gates, Buninovo, towards Gruz. We had meant to drop by and into the regional infirmary which is in the Gruz area, but it was closed at the time because of the shelling and because of the alarm. So we found no one there and we proceeded on to our house. The next day, I went to the infirmary for an examination and bandaging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to the Pilica Gate [sic]. Did you walk through Pile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the Od Puca Street, through Stradun, and the Pile Gate, towards Buninovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you walk home with your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we walked home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the shelling still continuing when you were walking through the Old Town, Pile, to Gruz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. By 11.30, the shelling had stopped and explosions could no longer be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go the next day for your examination and bandaging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I went to this infirmary in Gruz, the regional clinic in Gruz, in which there were nurses and a physician, and there they dressed my wound and I returned home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you require any ongoing treatment for your two wounds, on your chin and on your leg? Did you go back to the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I returned for perhaps another couple of times, two times; the second and the third day for a new bandage, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a war disability pension or make a claim for one as a result of receiving these injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither did I apply for one nor did I get anything for it because I didn't apply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the physical injuries. Now, what about psychological injuries? How did you feel in the first few weeks after experiencing the explosion, the injury, and the death of Tonci Skocko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can imagine. Not only that night but for days I was really under a very difficult impression. First of all, one experienced disbelief because one couldn't really fathom that this kind of thing had happened to a person who had only started living, as it were, and that you had lost him. His father was unable to go to work having experienced this trauma and this intense pain. And one would wake up at night, one couldn't sleep, one kept reliving the events of that day in one's mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you feel about having gone out with Tonci, that young man, that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel afterwards about you and him having gone out, outside, during the shelling that day? What did you feel about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a long time I myself felt this sense of guilt as if I myself had been to blame for the late Tonci's death because I was together with him at that particular moment. We had gone out together, so I kept having these self-recriminating feelings even though, of course, I had nothing to do with it and it was obvious who was to blame, but I still felt this guilt, thinking along the lines why did we have to go out? Why did this thing have to happen to precisely him? So it was a very ugly feeling, a difficult feeling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any sort of psychological counselling or assistance for these feelings you experienced afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was no need, really. And I imagine myself to be a more or less stable person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how did you manage to overcome these feelings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, time heals everything. You get on with your life, and you realise that it wasn't only you, that the same thing had happened to a lot of people and that a lot of people had fared far worse with their relatives getting killed. And then you have to think about Mato, what his feelings were. You have to hold back. At least, whenever I met him, I had to try to act normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mato close the shop after this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day and the next day -- for two days after. Two days later there was the funeral when Tonci Skocko was buried, so the shop remained closed for two or three days, and then we resumed work as usual. My sister, I, and a woman, a lady named Silva who worked with us, and Mato came back to work perhaps a fortnight later. We kept the shop up and running for two weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to describe what you saw as you walked through the Old Town with your sister after the shelling on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the whole thing settled down and when shells stopped falling, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the first thing we did when we went out onto the street, our street was a disaster. It was a mess. Many things had been destroyed, houses on both sides. The walls were pimpled from shrapnel. You could see destruction to the stone walls and the windows had been shattered. Just across the way there was another house, the facade of which was made of stone, and you could see even more holes and damage. On our way down to the elementary school building, we could see people leaving the shelter. The whole house had caught fire just across the way from the elementary school building. There was rubble all over the place, curtains falling down. And then just opposite the Orthodox church there is a huge palace, three or four floors high, and about 50 metres long, and the whole building was ablaze. It was a disaster to look at. There were people standing outside. An elderly man was crying, sitting there on the floor. He had perhaps devoted most of his life to the reconstruction and preservation of that building, and the yet whole thing disappeared into thin air in a matter of minutes. There was rubble in the streets, unexploded shells. The palace on Siroka Street was also on fire, a large building. There was another building on the Stradun which was also on fire. The Dubrovnik summer festival building, where many valuable things were being kept, and those had burnt too. The entire Old Town was covered in smoke. And the fire brigade started arriving, and they couldn't even move about from all the debris, from all the rubble and everything burning. The situation was disastrous in the Old Town. People had started coming out into the street, staring in disbelief at what had happened. This is a situation which I still find very difficult to describe. It's beyond words, everything that happened in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your -- in the street in which your shop was located, that's Miha Pracata, you described damage to the stone facades. Which side of the street had the stone facades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the houses. I think about 90 per cent of the houses had stone facades. Those were all made of stone. But just across from my shop there is a house with a concrete facade. All of the other houses in the Old Town are made of stone. So that the house with the concrete facade shows even better the destruction. On a different street, the staircase had been shattered because several shells fell there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and tumbled down the stairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in relation to the stone facades in the street of your shop, and the cement facade, how did the damage to the cement facade compare to that on the stone facades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the concrete facade showed the extent of the destruction a lot better because stone is hard. So, yes, you can see damage to the stone around the doors and the windows, but the concrete shows this better because the holes are larger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the difference between the damage to the cement facade and the stone facades? What was different about the damage to the cement facade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, actually, if you look at the cement facade, the damage looks greater. The holes look bigger. But that facade is easier to make than the stone facade, because when a stone building is damaged, you have to replace whole slabs of stones so it appears to be less damage than the cement facade but actually the damage is much heavier than that which occurred to the cement facade, where the holes look bigger

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the street in which your shop was located, was there -- was the damage to each side of the buildings on each side of the street more or less equal or was there some difference between the damage on the different sides of the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the streets in the Old Town, even my street, the whole thing is perhaps about a metre or two across. So those are narrow little streets. So you can't say which one was damaged more than the other. The house where our shop was, we only found out the following day there was a direct point of impact in the roof. It was hit directly through the roof. So we can't say that one side of the street was damaged more than the other. It was the same intensity throughout. It was a very narrow street, so the damage was more or less equal on both sides of the street. The street is not very wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said that your building was hit directly through the roof. Can you describe the -- describe the damage to the roof, such as the dimensions of the hole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the impact on the roof, the direct impact, that was at the far end of the roof, and the hole was two, two and a half metres across, I guess. There were shells that fell right down through the house, but the one that exploded on the roof, there was only damage to the roof and the attic -- the first floor, rather, from up above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other damage was there to the shop building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the roof had been hit. The curtains had been burned due to the two explosions in the street outside. The shutters and the windows on the house and then the door and the windows on the ground floor had been shattered. So everything had to be replaced. The damage had been considerable. But in comparison to some other houses, it was quite insignificant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The shop was on the ground floor, there was a house upstairs. How many floors does this building have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So there was a shop on the ground floor, there was another floor, and an attic with a -- what is usually called Belvedere. It's the sort of thing you very often find in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what a Belvedere is? Describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's the local name we use in Dubrovnik. You have something just underneath the roof protruding, sticking out. There are windows and Venetian blinds so that if there is someone living in the attic, in order to make a flat up there and in order to have enough air, the roof was slanted, and Belvedere means a view. So there was a view, and those were made to bring enough sun to the attic flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the door flying open when a shell landed and windows breaking. Was there any damage to the door of the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door had been shattered totally and damaged by shrapnel, and the other part of the door that was on the hinges, it came off the hinges due to the explosion and was broken. So the whole door was demolished and had to be replaced. It was -- it had been pierced by shrapnel, and there were holes in the wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the door made of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door was made of wood. It was the same in all the houses in the Old Town. The only two materials you find are wood and stone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the inside of the shop damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just behind the door there was a counter with a till, the phone, that sort of thing, the sort of thing you find there. The till had been damaged, broken. Part of the counter itself, the shells inside where provisions were kept, those that were near the door had also been damaged. So there was a lot of damage in terms of what was inside the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there people living upstairs on the day of this attack, that is the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first floor there was an old lady living there who had -- who died five or six years ago. She slept all the time -- I think for two or three months she slept at the Revelin fort. She would sometimes walk home during the day. She would do some cleaning, and she would regularly go back to the Revelin fort because that's where she slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether she was home on the day of the -- day of the attack, that is the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is no, you don't know; or no, she wasn't home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. I don't think she was home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also described damage to a staircase. Is there a staircase in the street the shop's located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the staircase you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one I had in mind. It's outside in the street, and then the street goes up towards the Old Town, St. Mary. That's what it's called, and that's -- that's where there is a staircase. In the Old Town, practically all the streets are on a slope with the possible exception of the Stradun, but all the other streets have stairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was that staircase damaged on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the whole staircase, two shells had landed directly on that staircase, and the steps were demolished. There was a crater where the two shells fell. So the steps -- the stone steps were broken all around and damaged, those that were higher up. So there was a lot of damage there too. It was very difficult to go down, to walk down that street on the day after everything had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is the staircase from the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It -- just outside the shop, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the building opposite the Orthodox church which you saw on fire on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the name is. It's a huge palace. I think probably the name is indicated on the map. I know where it is, but I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also described another palace being ablaze. Do you know the name of that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that one was on fire, and the one on Siroka Street was on fire too. There were shops on the ground floor there, and now there's a post office. Another building that was on fire was the one on the Stradun, the Dubrovnik summer festival building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This damage you've just described seeing on the 6th of December in the Old Town, was that there on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. There was none of it on the 5th of December. It was only earlier on in October those two shells landed, I think. It was in Miha Pracata Street. But those two incidents are completely unrelated. This was the Old Town. And after the shelling, it no longer looked like the Old Town. It was just ruins and smoke, fire, rubble. It looked like anything else that I might think of, but it was no longer the Old Town that we used to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any United Nations or UNESCO flags in the Old Town before the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Old Town, on the Orlando column, on Fort Minceta, on Fort Lovrijenac, on Fort Boka, at the Pile Gate, up on the bastion where we had Croatian flags and still do, but I think as early as October and November the Croatian flags had been taken down and UNESCO flags had been hoisted up, and UN flags too. The Sponza Palace, too, sported a flag. The rector's palace, the Little Brethren monastery. The Dominican monastery had flags. It was marked as a monument of culture. But all of this, apparently, was of no use, because many people who lived in the surrounding areas, in Gruz, in Lapad, who had friends or relatives in the Old Town had moved to the Old Town to stay there because they believed that the Old Town would be safe from harm, that it would never be targeted. Unfortunately, it happened. So all those important buildings in the Old Town had been marked long before the whole thing happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm showing the witness a copy of the Prosecution Exhibit P13, which is the large map of the Old Town. I'll ask him to mark various things on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, can you find -- can you find your shop on the map? Just point to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shop is on Miha Pracata Street. The -- further down the street, I could mark it if you want me to, it's past Nikola Gucetica Street and Pecarica Street, that's where the shop is, halfway through the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to take a pen, and I want you to draw an A, the first letter of the alphabet, in circle. Actually, don't do a circle, just draw a little square. Draw a square where the shop is and put an A inside it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now with a B, I want to you mark -- just wait until I tell you exactly. I want to you mark where you and Tonci were when the shell landed, and I also want you to put an arrow facing in the direction in which you were facing. Do you follow what I mean? A B for where you were standing and an arrow for the direction in which you were facing or standing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to put a C for the stairs that you described, or maybe you could even draw the stairs in. They're not actually marked on this particular map. The stone stairs at the end of the street.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's right here where the street begins and where it ends, and this is where it cuts across Nikola Gucetica Street, and then there's a staircase up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just draw some lines across the street to indicate the staircase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want you to mark is where the shells landed and damaged that staircase. Don't draw it over the B. Perhaps if you put the C -- just stop. Perhaps if you put the C just to the left where the buildings are, with an arrow pointing down to it, in the same way you've drawn the

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Put the C off the street, with an arrow pointing to the spot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned you saw a house on fire near the elementary school. Could you please mark that, again with a box and a D. That is the house on fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the Orthodox church on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can't see it here, but you can see the block of buildings where the church is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's right here near the number 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark that with an E, that is, where you saw the building opposite the Orthodox church burning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Letter E?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned another palace whose name you didn't give us which was burning. Can you mark that on the map, too, please, with an F.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that next to the post office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's just where the post office is today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned some other buildings which you saw on fire. Can you mark the next one with a G.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the building you've just marked with a G?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is the Dubrovnik summer festival building. I'm not sure what the official name of the palace is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see any other buildings on fire; and if so, can you mark it with an H.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I came out of the building, there was nothing on fire there any longer, only the Hotel Opat [phoen] Pile. I think it's the Ana Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that outside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to mark it on the side with a legend, Your Honour, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H? Maybe, maybe not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it can be done, perhaps during the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please put your name down the bottom, just on the bottom of the map somewhere, write your name, sign your name, and put today's date, which is the 23rd of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would that be an appropriate time, and it could be marked during the interval?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand during the break that court officials have made some markings on the map. Could I just have a look at it, please. And on it is written A, Mr. Jovic's shop; B, location where Jovic and Tonci stood when shell landed, arrow indicates direction they were facing; C, staircase with arrows where shells landed and damaged staircase; D, location of house near elementary school on fire; E, location of building near Orthodox church which was burning; F, location of palace near post office which was burning; G, other buildings on fire (Dubrovnik summer festival building); and H, there's nothing next to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which brings me to H, Mr. Jovic, just before we broke. I'm not quite sure if it's completely clarified: Were there any other buildings which you saw burning in the Old Town which you could mark on that map with an H?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the Old Town, there probably were. There were a lot of damaged houses because only few houses did not suffer a few -- or some hits. I only drew here the houses which I saw at the moment we were leaving Old Town and were homebound, for which I'm sure -- which I'm sure were on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that map be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P75.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, how many employees did Mato Skocko have as of the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, we in the shop were I myself, my sister, his son Tonci, and Mato Skocko. There was another lady by the name of Silva. I'm not sure of her last name. She wasn't an employee. She also worked in the Lapad area but didn't show up for work on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to -- I'm sorry. Did you go back to the Old Town the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did. After I -- I had gone to Gruz to have my wound dressed, then we went to Old Town again, but already there were several thousand people on the Stradun who had come to see what had happened, so at a certain point the city was overcrowded with people who were cleaning up, and in these old houses which -- these old houses which have been set on fire were still smouldering. The city was in a disastrous state. One could only then see what had really happened. All the cross streets were buried under the rubble, the debris, the timber, the brick that had fallen, the tiles that had fallen off the roofs, and the Stradun was a veritable dump, garbage dump. That is how the main street of the town looked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you assist in the clean-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What repairs were made to Mato Skocko's shop as a result of the attack on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 7th or perhaps in the afternoon of the 7th, or the same day on the 7th or in the morning of the 7th, the -- some people came who just carried out makeshift repairs on the door, just boarded them up -- them up rather -- it up, rather, before the new door was installed, and then they changed, replaced the till because the old one was no longer usable. Then they took away some crates with shattered glass because the bottles had been all shattered by the explosion. So we cleaned on that day and on the 8th and resumed normal work on the 9th or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the effect of the UN and UNESCO flags in the Old Town on the people of Dubrovnik and the people of the Old Town? Sorry, the morale of the people of the Old Town of Dubrovnik itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UNESCO and United Nations flags which had been hoisted on the ramparts and the forts around the Old Town and the protected cultural monument buildings actually instilled some confidence and a feeling of security in the citizens, because the citizens thought because of that, as did I, that because of that the city was not be targeted or shelled. In fact, they not only thought that this would not happen, but also that the international community and the rest of the world would protect the Old City. Regrettably, that did not -- that's not the way it turned out to be. So that people lost faith in the United Nations as well as all these other institutions which were supposed to protect them but didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you knew in October, November, and December, up until the 6th of December, 1991, were there any military installations or mortars located in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were -- not that there were no mortars in the Old Town. There were no -- there was no -- there were no troops. There was no army. Perhaps a soldier or two would show up in town because they came home on furlough, but there were no military positions in the Old Town of Dubrovnik at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Will Mr. Usher please give me the lectern. Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovic, good morning. I'm Goran Rodic, an attorney-at-law. I shall be asking you some questions in connection with the testimony which you have given. At the outset, I should like to ask you, since we speak a similar language, to wait until my question has been translated so that we do not overlap and make the work of the interpreters difficult. Can you tell me, where exactly do you reside in Gruz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stjepan Cvijica Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a family house, a residential house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you live with there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean then or now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was me, my wife, my daughter, my mother, and my grandmother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that immediately prior to the beginning of this war you started working in this shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you completed your military service in 1993, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to Dubrovnik, were you assigned to a war duty station, and to what unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was assigned to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what particular assignment did you have in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the same thing as the training that I had received in the army, which is the -- an operator of Maljutkas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period from 1983 to 1991, did you participate in any military exercises as a reservist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I only was there twice in Trebinje, that is, in the Trebinje barracks, where we had such trainings for the Maljutka. It was a sort of training drill, and we had those on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then as a reservist in the Territorial Defence, were you a part of the Trebinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. This was the Dubrovnik Territorial Defence. That is what it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the -- you were issued the call-up, the mobilisation summons from the military commission, which was brought to you by the postman who had also been mobilised, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was what I said. He probably had also been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something more specific about when the general mobilisation, general call-up was declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mobilisation started sometime before, perhaps already around the time -- around the end of September, rather, the 25th, 26th, or 27th of November, by the time the attacks on Konavle had started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the general mobilisation publicised through the media in any way; via radio, television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- did general mobilisation involve all men fit for service? Were they supposed to report to the nearest duty stations or units or military departments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, those who received the -- were issued with such call-up summons actually did report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when general mobilisation is in question, the people can report also without being summoned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that -- that you received the summons at home and then that you responded either -- or, rather, that you -- the station to which you were supposed to report was in Gruz at the Hotel Stadion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there at the Hotel Stadion also -- were there also a number of members of the National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, no. As far as I know, they were at the Vila Rasica, the National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any units or positions around the Hotel Stadion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you departed that place, the Hotel Stadion, when you were sent to Rasica, were you not put up at the Hotel Vrtovi Sunca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were. Excuse me. No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not quite sure what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, because of a mistake in the transcript, were you transferred from the Hotel Stadion to Orasac, and were you accommodated there at the Vrtovi Sunca Hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Stadion hotel, the five or six of us who were there went on a -- in a private car to Orasac, to the Vrtovi Sunca Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any members of the Croatian National Guard there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that it was only the five of you who were at the -- represented at the Hotel Vrtovi Sunca and in the area generally speaking, some soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we were, what we represented, whether we were soldiers, that is hard to say. We were sent there for -- in order for the army or the police to bring us these Maljutkas, but we had no weapons, we had no uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you supposed to use these Maljutkas to open fire at the JNA gunboat if you received them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't tell me it was just five of you who were supposed to fight against JNA battleships.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that that was why we were sent there. Now, of course the army which was around was not in Orasac yet because Orasac was not liberated yet. Maybe towards the area of Slano there were some soldiers. But there were none in Orasac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were -- where were the closest positions of the Croatian army, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of Slano, as far as I know. Down there towards Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was supposed to give you these Maljutkas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably someone was supposed to drive them up to that point, and we were there waiting at the Hotel Vrtovi Sunca. There was no electricity at that time. We were sleeping there, and we had our meals also there because -- and of course lots of other people had begun to flock in as refugees because they were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who were supposed to bring the Maljutkas to you, how would that someone make a distinction between you and the refugees who were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They knew where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it that was supposed to bring them to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably someone from the Civil Defence, the Territorial Defence, the police. Someone was supposed to bring them and then give them to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was to give you your instructions as to your mission, as to your task and your concrete operation against the -- and the positions that you would take with these weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were supposed to establish such positions ourselves on -- and this person who had this van also was supposed to take us there, and we were supposed to establish position vis-a-vis the two ships in the channel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do any reconnaissance of the terrain while you were waiting for the Maljutkas to see where the most favourable location would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We walked around, but we didn't identify or find the specific position until getting the Maljutkas -- and we didn't get the Maljutkas, so it all ended there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- would these Maljutkas have been delivered to you at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably not at the hotel. Probably somewhere along the road or the coast, and then we would take them in the van or the car to the point desired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where can one approach by car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the sea line, to the sea coast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then should your position from which to open fire, should it have been somewhere close to the sea, close to the coast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it should have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these positions prepared beforehand or would you be using existing structures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing was prepared beforehand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I imagine you would not be opening fire from the beach.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps we would have been, because one really didn't know. You had a ship which was sailing in the channel, which was opening fire at civilians and trucks perhaps. Who knows what concrete positions we would have adopted had we received those weapons and from which point we would have opened fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't believe in your military training that you completed with the JNA --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you were trained to open fire from a Maljutka unprotected vis-a-vis the target that you were targeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a different time. You couldn't really apply everything that you learned in the army and dig trenches around Orasac in order to be able to follow a particular principle in order to open fire at those ships.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who sent you there specifically? Who sent you to Orasica on that mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those people from the recruitment office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who specifically? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. I don't know. I don't know what their names were. Right now I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you not remember a single name, someone you were in touch with about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the recruitment office where the people were who sent you to Orasica [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is its location, the location of the recruitment office who told you to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's -- the distance is about 500 metres from the Stadion Hotel where we were staying. It's near Buninovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the general direction of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who called you there to receive your tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This gentleman walked down to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which gentleman was that? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a soldier wearing a uniform? Did he have any rank displayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a civilian at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that man personally before this mission, before this situation that we have spoken about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come he knew exactly who -- who to speak to and how you would meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps he knew my first and last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone call out names when they came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he came, he was looking specifically for the four or five of us who were there, because we had been called up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who in that group should have been the commander, should have been in charge, should have told the others what to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was not the main thing. It wasn't a proper army. There was no such structure in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that among the five of you everyone was free to do whatever they liked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, in a way. Anyone could have just walked off. Anyone could have decided not to join us. They were free to do so. No one was forced to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you receive a mobilisation call, it's some kind of obligation, isn't it? It's compulsory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I suppose, but that was a very different time and there were strange things happening down there. What befell Dubrovnik at the time was a war we had not been prepared for. We had not seen it coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you took an Atlas boat to go to Babin Kuk on your way back from Orasac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of an Atlas boat was that? Was that a tourist boat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, then, what about the Croatian navy? Had it been commandeered by the Croatian navy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was used for the transport of civilians from Orasac back to the town. That's what it was used for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it used to transport soldiers too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did you do back in Babin Kuk? Which unit was it that was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was no unit, really, nor did we do anything particular there. We just got off the boat there. We reached the Stadion Hotel to see who we should speak to there, who we should report to and how, but some of the people had already left for their positions, and we didn't find anyone there. So a man came along and told us sort of to -- to go up to the recruitment office and see what we should do, and then we went there and we found some official or other who couldn't tell us what to do or where to go. So that's why I went back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this Atlas boat, instead of going to Babin Kuk, why didn't it go straight to the Gruz harbour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably that was the quickest route. This way it was able to make two or three rounds a day and transport more people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- this man you reported to later at the recruitment office, was that a different person from the person who sent you to Orasica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was yet another person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to one of the questions by the OTP, you said that on the 4th or 5th of October you reported back to the command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by the time I got back I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what sort of a command that was and who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, when we were back, we had been in Orasac. We had been there for three or four -- well, actually the 1st of October, when the attack began, the attack against the town, then we were off to Orasica and stayed there for three or four days, and on the 4th, when Slano had fallen, the civilians from the surrounding villages were fleeing Slano and they were going to Dubrovnik. Most of those had arrived at the Vrtovi Sunca Hotel, and then we went back and there was a van there, and it remained where it was at Zaton. We went to Babin Kuk on the 4th, and then we reported to this whatever its name was, the recruitment office up there where this command was. Now, whether it was the command of the town defence or not, I don't know, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander at that specific command where you reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
